info.title: HelloBooks Public API
info.summary: Third-party accounting API for HelloBooks organisations.
info.description:
Machine-readable description of the HelloBooks public API, **generated** from the route registry rather than written by hand. Regenerate with `node scripts/generate-openapi.js`; `tests/publicApiOpenapi.test.js` fails the build when a live route has no entry here.

## What this document is honest about

Response and request **field lists are not published yet**. The field contract that would supply them (`routes/publicApi.contract.js`) is present (routes/publicApi.contract.js); 76 of 105 resources have a published field baseline, and its generated baseline is deliberately empty at increment 1. Rather than emit confident empty schemas, every unresolved shape here is an unconstrained object marked `x-hellobooks-field-contract: "unpublished"`. Absence of properties means *not yet described*, never *no fields*.

## Authentication and scopes

OAuth 2.0 authorization code. The access token carries the `marketplace_app` audience and is bound to a single AppInstall, and so to a single (org, entity) pair.

Scopes are granular: **14 domains x {read, write} = 28 scopes**, plus the two legacy bundles. Each of the 466 factory operations names the scope of its own resource domain — `sales:read` for an invoice, `payroll:read` for an employee, `paymentmethods:read` for a stored card — so a token scoped to sales cannot reach payroll or card details at all.

`book:read` and `book:write` remain **grantable bundle scopes**, not deprecated aliases: `book:read` expands to every `<domain>:read` and `book:write` to every `<domain>:write` (never to reads). Each operation's `security` therefore lists the granular scope AND the bundle that satisfies it as alternatives, which is how a generated client learns both grants are valid. The full domain table and both expansions are in `components.securitySchemes.marketplaceOAuth2.x-hellobooks-scope-model`.

Two surfaces stay coarse deliberately: dynamic client registration and the `/books/drafts` flow require only the bundles, because AI-MCP-Hellobooks understands exactly four scope strings and a granular scope would grant its connector nothing. Those operations are marked `x-hellobooks-scope-grain: "coarse-bundle"`.

No scope is required for `GET /health`, `GET /me` — service endpoints that carry no tenant payload. They are still behind the bearer token; there is no anonymous endpoint on this gateway.

## Tenancy

Every resource path carries `{orgId}` and `{entityId}`. `requireTenantParamMatch` rejects any value that is not the install's own OrgRefId / EntityRefId with 403 `tenant_scope_violation`. `GET /me` is how a client discovers the pair it is allowed to use.

## Rate limits

Counted per `(clientId, installId)`. Default **120 requests / 60 seconds**, overridable per app via `AppApiKey.RateLimit.MaxRequests`; when no override exists and plan enforcement is switched on, the ceiling comes from the org plan's `ApiRequestsPerMinute`. On failure of the limiter's Redis store the request is allowed through (`passOnStoreError`). Responses carry RFC 9651 draft-8 `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers; a 429 adds `Retry-After`.

## Billing

Every request except `/health`, `/me` and the books draft→commit flow is pre-charged against the tenant's AI-credit wallet and settles only on a response below 400. A depleted wallet returns 402.

## Error shapes

There are **two**, and they are not interchangeable. Gateway middlewares return `{ error: "<code>", message }` where `error` is a string. Plan-entitlement denials return `{ success: false, error: { code, plan, upgradeTo, upgradeUrl, feature } }` where `error` is an object. Both can arrive on 403. Clients must branch on the type of `error` before reading it.

get.summary: List account records
get.description: Mounted by the generic resource factory in `routes/publicApi.routes.js` from the registry row `account` in `routes/publicApi.resources.js`. The request is delegated to the SAME internal controller a signed-in user hits (`controllers/GRPC/Accounting/account.grpc` → `getAccounts`), so it inherits that controller's validation, server-side tax computation and audit trail. Guards applied, in order: bearer token (`marketplace_app` audience) → plan API-access entitlement → rate limit → AI-credit metering → permission context of the installing user → tenant path match → `requireScope("accounting:read")`.

get.summary: Fetch events for a pull-mode subscription
get.description:
Cursor-based and NON-CONSUMING. `after` is the last `delivery_id` you successfully handled; everything newer comes back, oldest first. Asking again with the same cursor returns the same events — which is the point: an app that crashes between fetching and handling has lost nothing, where a fetch-and-consume queue would have dropped that event silently.

At-least-once, with a stable `event_id` to de-duplicate on. That is the same contract push mode has.

Each event carries the `headers` a push delivery would have carried, signed at THIS handover rather than when the event was recorded — an event that waited six minutes in the queue would otherwise arrive already outside the five-minute freshness window, and a correctly written receiver would reject its own first event. So verification code written against this endpoint is the code that runs in production.

`next_cursor` is absent-as-unchanged on an empty page: a poller holds its existing cursor rather than resetting to the start of the queue.

409 if the subscription is push mode — its events were POSTed to `target_url`, so read them from the delivery log instead. 404 if no such subscription belongs to this app.

marketplaceOAuth2.description:
Authorization-code OAuth 2.0 against the HelloBooks marketplace provider. The access token's audience is `marketplace_app`; it is bound to one AppInstall, and therefore to exactly one (org, entity) pair. Public clients use PKCE (`code_challenge` / `code_challenge_method` are accepted on /oauth/authorize).

Scopes are GRANULAR: 14 domains x {read, write} = 28 scopes, derived from the internal RBAC permission entity each of the 100 registry resources already gates on, folded onto the module axis of the RBAC v2 manifest. `book:read` and `book:write` are NOT deprecated and NOT removed — they remain first-class grantable BUNDLE scopes that expand to every granular read / write scope respectively, which is why every token issued before this vocabulary existed keeps working unchanged. Request the narrowest domains you need; ask for a bundle only if you genuinely need the whole surface.

book:read.description: Read all of your books data (legacy bundle — grants every read scope)

book:write.description: Create and update all of your books data (legacy bundle — grants every write scope)

compatibilityRules: `book:write` expands to every `<domain>:write`. It deliberately does NOT expand to reads — a write-only token cannot reach a read route today, and that stays true.

Webhook subscription management was gated by nothing beyond a valid bearer token, so `webhooks:read` + `webhooks:write` are granted to any token carrying either bundle AND to any token carrying no granular public-API scope at all. That covers live installs on unrelated vocabularies. Only a NEW grant that opted into granular scopes is held to them.
x-hellobooks-scope-model.expansionIsCheckedAtTheGuard: middlewares/appAccessToken.middleware.js expands the granted list before requireScope() tests it, and never rewrites it: GET /me still reports exactly what was granted, not the expansion.
coarseByDesign: POST /oauth/register (dynamic client registration) grants only the two bundles.
The /books/drafts draft -> confirm -> commit routes require only the bundles.
Both because AI-MCP-Hellobooks understands exactly four scope strings and ignores the rest, so a granular scope would grant its connector nothing.

notGrantableOnThisApi.reason: Part of the marketplace catalog and enforced by AI-MCP-Hellobooks, but checked by no /public/v1 route. Listing them among this API's scopes would imply they grant something here. They do not.

orgId.name: orgId
orgId.description: The organisation the call targets. MUST equal the OrgRefId the access token's AppInstall is bound to — `requireTenantParamMatch` returns 403 `tenant_scope_violation` otherwise. There is no cross-tenant form of this API.

entityId.name: entityId
entityId.description: The entity (book) within the organisation. MUST equal the install's EntityRefId; see `orgId`.

webhookSubscriptionId.name: id
webhookSubscriptionId.description:
Identifier of a webhook subscription, as returned by POST /webhooks. A 24-character hex ObjectId -- these records live in Mongo, unlike the accounting resources whose ids are UUIDs.

The pattern is not decoration: `deliveries` and `topics` are reserved sub-collections under /webhooks, and it is what makes `/webhooks/{id}/…` provably unable to capture them.

deliveryId.name: deliveryId
deliveryId.description: Identifier of a webhook delivery attempt, as returned by the delivery log.

draftId.name: draftId
draftId.description: Bookkeeping draft identifier returned by the draft create call.

isArchived.name: isArchived
isArchived.description: Return archived records instead of active ones. The gateway compares the raw query value against the literal string `true`; every other value, `1` and `TRUE` included, is treated as false.

GatewayError.description: The error shape emitted by the /public/v1 gateway middlewares (authentication, tenant match, scope, rate limit, controller binding).

required.description: Present on `insufficient_scope`: the scopes that were missing.

handler.description: Present on `handler_missing`: the controller export that was absent.

EntitlementError.description: A SECOND, DIFFERENT error shape. Plan-entitlement denials (`requireApiAccessFeature`) do not use the gateway shape above — they return the first-party subscription-guard payload, in which `error` is an OBJECT rather than a string. A client that reads `body.error` as a string will get `[object Object]` here. This divergence is real and is described rather than smoothed over.

AiCreditsError.description: AI-credit metering refusal. Every /public/v1 request except /health, /me and the books draft→commit flow is charged against the install's tenant AI-credit wallet before any tenant work happens.

SuccessEnvelope.description: A /public/v1 success body. THERE IS NO SINGLE ENVELOPE — this was measured, not assumed: across the Accounting controllers these routes delegate to, top-level success keys are `success` (219 sites), `message` (322), `data` (18), plus 146 distinct resource-named keys such as `accounts`, `bills`, `transactions`, `items`, `groups`. Any rule of the form 'the payload lives under .data' would be wrong most of the time. The properties below are therefore the keys that MAY appear, none of them required, and the payload itself sits under a resource-named key this description cannot yet name per resource.

x-hellobooks-generated.doNotEdit: Regenerate with `node scripts/generate-openapi.js`. tests/publicApiOpenapi.test.js fails if this file is edited by hand or left stale.

inputs.scopeVocabulary: utils/publicApiScopes.util.js — every operation's scope is produced by that module's scopeFor(), never synthesised here
inputs.fieldContract: present (routes/publicApi.contract.js); 76 of 105 resources have a published field baseline

knownGaps: Field-level request/response schemas are unpublished for every resource (empty contract baseline).
`owner:close` and `audit:export` remain in the marketplace catalog but gate no /public/v1 route; they are enforced by AI-MCP-Hellobooks only.

55 pairs of path templates overlap — one URL can match both. 54 are the resource factory's `/{id}` vs `/restore` shape; 1 involve a parameter at a different position. Express resolves them by registration order. All are method-disjoint, so no request is actually routed ambiguously. Full list in x-hellobooks-generated.pathTemplateOverlaps.
Success bodies use resource-named top-level keys rather than one envelope, so the payload key is not described per operation.

No business event is ever enqueued for webhook delivery — MEASURED: the delivery worker starts unconditionally and POSTs with an HMAC signature, but nothing in the codebase produces a job for it. A subscription therefore receives no callbacks on its own. The only deliveries that occur are those an app triggers itself through the test and replay endpoints, which do send for real.
